nodes.title: MAST: 14 failure modes in 3 categories, human kappa 0.88, LLM judge F1 0.80
nodes.body: MAST (Cemri et al., arXiv:2503.13657, NeurIPS 2025 spotlight) is the reference error taxonomy for agentic runs: 200+ traces from 7 multi-agent frameworks, 6 expert annotators, 14 failure modes grouped into specification issues, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification. Human inter-annotator agreement took three rounds to stabilize (Cohen kappa 0.24, then 0.92, then 0.84) and the headline figure is kappa 0.88 on 15 triple-annotated traces, with 0.79 on unseen systems. An o1 LLM judge validates at 0.89 accuracy / 0.62 recall / 0.68 precision / 0.64 F1 / 0.58 kappa zero-shot, rising to 0.94 / 0.77 / 0.833 / 0.80 / 0.77 few-shot. Its central claim is exactly ours: failures are organizational and design-level, not base-model limits. But note the judge's recall, 0.62 to 0.77: two to four in ten failures are missed, and the taxonomy's own category set has no bucket for a dead parent session or a worktree that failed to create.
nodes.source: arXiv:2503.13657 (Cemri et al., NeurIPS 2025), 200+ traces, 7 MAS frameworks, 14 modes / 3 categories, human kappa 0.88 headline (0.24 -> 0.92 -> 0.84 over rounds), o1 judge F1 0.64 zero-shot / 0.80 few-shot; github.com/multi-agent-systems-failure-taxonomy/MAST

nodes.title: TRAIL is the only published taxonomy with explicit infrastructure categories, and the best model scores 11%
nodes.body: TRAIL (Deshpande et al., Patronus AI, arXiv:2505.08638v3) is the taxonomy that matters for a harness: 148 human-annotated traces, 1987 OpenTelemetry spans of which 575 carry at least one error, drawn from GAIA and SWE-bench. Its three top areas are reasoning, planning/coordination, and system execution, and it is explicit that system execution includes API errors and task orchestration errors, i.e. the infrastructure bucket that MAST and the software-engineering taxonomies fold into nothing. The benchmark is brutally hard: gemini-2.5-pro, the best of o3, claude-3.7-sonnet and gemini-2.5-pro, reaches only 11% joint accuracy on predicting both the error category and its span location. That 11% is the honest ceiling for LLM-as-judge failure triage on structured traces, and it is measured on a task easier than ours because the trace format is already normalized.

nodes.title: Human-labelled cause split: 65% flawed reasoning, 25% knowledge, 10% environment
nodes.body: Liu et al. (arXiv:2509.13941) hand-labelled 150 failures sampled from 329 failed SWE-bench-Verified instances (95% confidence, 5% margin) into 3 phases (Location, Repair, Iteration & Validation), 9 categories and 25 subcategories, with Cohen kappa 0.72-0.77 across 4 annotators and under 8% of disagreements escalated to a senior adjudicator. Their cause distribution is the number our topic needs: flawed reasoning about 65%, knowledge deficiency about 25%, environmental friction about 10%. That 10% is the human estimate of non-model fault for a well-instrumented benchmark, and it is roughly consistent with dsh-loom's own 13.6% infra-flagged share of failures, which is the first evidence that the ledger's narrow label is not wildly wrong, only incomplete. They also show that the same backbone (Claude-3.5-Sonnet) scores 53.0% under OpenHands, 50.8% under Agentless and 49.0% under a tool-augmented Claude, a 4.0-point harness gap with the model held fixed.
nodes.source: arXiv:2509.13941 (Liu et al., Beihang), 150 of 329 failed instances labelled, kappa 0.72-0.77, cause split 65/25/10, OpenHands 53.0% / Agentless 50.8% / Tools+Claude 49.0% on the same backbone

nodes.title: The modal failure is not 'cannot find the code' but 'edited the right place wrongly' (60-69%)
nodes.body: TRAJEVAL / Coherence Collapse (arXiv:2603.24631v2) analyses 16,758 trajectories over 3 architectures (SWE-Agent, OpenHands, LiveSWEAgent) and 7 models from 8B to 480B on SWE-bench Verified and PolyBench Verified, and finds that 60-69% of failures on SWE-Agent and OpenHands reach and edit the correct functions yet produce an incorrect patch. The effect persists at 57-68% on bash-only LiveSWEAgent, so it is not a tool-schema artifact. Coherence Collapse is the largest sub-theme at 39.7% of 914 hand-analysed failures on SWE-bench Verified and 32.3% on PolyBench (Java 36.3%, JavaScript 42.1%). Five cases produced a patch bit-identical to gold mid-trajectory and then destroyed it; an edit-commit checkpoint recovers all five. For attribution this is decisive: the failure is neither localization (the agent was in the right place) nor a harness fault, so any classifier that keys on 'found the right file' will mislabel two-thirds of capability failures as progress.

nodes.title: 63.75% of 'resolved' SWE-bench patches are suspicious; filtering drops 12.47% to 3.97%
nodes.body: SWE-Bench+ (Aleithan et al., arXiv:2410.06992) manually screened SWE-Agent+GPT-4 resolved instances and found 160 of 251 patches (63.75%) suspicious: 32.67% had the solution leaked into the issue text or comments, and 31.08% were weak-test passes, i.e. incorrect or incomplete fixes that nonetheless went green, with 24.70% of suspicious fixes attributable to weak tests specifically. Filtering both drops the solve rate from 12.47% to 3.97%, a 68% reduction, and over 94% of issues predate the model's knowledge cutoff so leakage is not a memorization story. This is the verifier as a false-positive source, which is the opposite direction from the usual 'the test was flaky and rejected a good patch' story: a verifier that passes a bad patch corrupts the ledger's labels silently, and a loop that learns from its verifier will learn to satisfy the verifier rather than the task.
nodes.source: arXiv:2410.06992 (Aleithan et al., 2024), 251 SWE-Agent+GPT-4 patches, 160 (63.75%) suspicious, 32.67% answer leak, 31.08% weak tests, 12.47% -> 3.97% after filtering, >94% issues predate cutoff

nodes.title: Verifier error structure beats verifier error rate: learnable false positives collapse the loop
nodes.body: Checking the Checkers (Gupta & Joshi, AISSA 2026, arXiv:2610.17824) surveys 58 studies of verifier noise in RLVR and reaches a claim that reorganises this whole topic: the structure of a verifier error matters more than its rate. Random errors mostly slow learning down, but false positives that the policy can learn to trigger cause plateau or even collapse, and they do so at low initial error rates. Whether a verifier wrongly rejects or wrongly accepts depends on what it checks and who built it, not on its family (unit test, LLM judge, static check). Applied to dsh-loom: our 8 literal '0/0 passed' attempts and 23 failureKind=ok-but-verifierOk=false attempts are not symmetric noise, they are a specific structure, and the vacuous-collection case is exactly the learnable kind because a worker that emits no tests inherits a green-looking exit path in some harness versions.
nodes.source: arXiv:2610.17824 (Gupta & Joshi, AISSA 2026), survey of 58 RLVR studies, claim: error structure (learnable false positives) dominates error rate, false positives cause plateau/collapse at low rates

nodes.title: Automated failure attribution tops out near 53% on which agent, ~14% on which step
nodes.body: Three independent results bracket the ceiling. Who&When (Zhang et al., ICML 2025, arXiv:2505.00212) collects 127 multi-agent failure logs with fine-grained annotations and finds the best of three automated methods at 53.5% accuracy for identifying the responsible agent and only 14.2% for the decisive error step; some methods fall below random, hand-crafted systems drop to 8.77% step accuracy, and the authors call o1 and DeepSeek-R1 not practically usable. AgenTracer (arXiv:2509.03312) reports state-of-the-art reasoning LLMs below 10% on agentic failure attribution. AgentChaos (ASE 2026, DOI 10.1145/3832783.3837437) finds existing fault diagnosis methods below 53% on fault type and below 56% on fault step under injected API faults. So a 53% ceiling is not one paper's bad day, it is the current state, and it means an LLM-judge triage layer cannot be the primary attribution mechanism for a loop that must decide where to spend.
nodes.source: arXiv:2505.00212 (Who&When, ICML 2025) 127 logs, 53.5% agent / 14.2% step, 8.77% hand-crafted; arXiv:2509.03312 (AgenTracer) SOTA <10%; AgentChaos ASE 2026 DOI 10.1145/3832783.3837437 <53% type / <56% step

nodes.title: FAMAS: spectrum-based suspiciousness beats 12 baselines without an LLM in the loop
nodes.body: FAMAS (Ge et al., arXiv:2509.13782, Nanjing University / PolyU) is the first spectrum-based failure attribution method for multi-agent systems, and it is the strongest evidence that attribution does not need a model. It replays trajectories systematically, abstracts them into agent-behaviour and action-behaviour groups, and ranks suspects with a suspiciousness formula borrowed from spectrum-based fault localisation (the same lineage as Tarantula/Ochiai). It beats 12 baselines on Who&When, including the LLM-judge methods that the 53.5%-and-below numbers above describe. The mechanism is the one a ledger naturally has: a set of passed and failed executions over sharing components, and a statistic on how often each component appears in failures but not in passes. dsh-loom already records exactly the substrate FAMAS needs (attempt id, model, chain position, patch paths, verifier outcome), which makes this the cheapest credible upgrade path and the one worth prototyping first.
nodes.source: arXiv:2509.13782 (Ge et al., 2025), spectrum-based failure attribution for MAS, systematic trajectory replay + abstraction, suspiciousness over agent-behaviour and action-behaviour groups, beats 12 baselines on Who&When

nodes.title: Scaffold choice moves scores 29.8 points while the model gap between top entries is 8.8
nodes.body: Coding Agents Have Converged (Liu et al., arXiv:2609.17394, ADMA 2026) analyses 254 SWE-bench submissions without running a single model. On Verified the top two entries each resolve 396/500; the top ten share 285 successes and 51 failures, leaving 164 instances that actually distinguish them, and frontier solution sets have median nesting 0.935 against a score-implied baseline of 0.774. The decisive number for attribution is that within-model scaffolds spread 29.8 percentage points while the top thirty entries spread only 8.8 points overall, so the harness is a larger cause of score than the model is. Six of nine cell-mean interaction tests stay significant after Holm correction, yet exact paired McNemar separates none of the 29 adjacent Verified top-thirty pairs at alpha 0.05. Translation: harness dominates in aggregate but is invisible pairwise on this task set, which is precisely why a loop that blames the model for a harness fault will chase a difference its own evaluation cannot resolve.

nodes.title: Single-run pass@1 swings 2.2-6.0 points, with standard deviation above 1.5 points at temperature 0
nodes.body: On Randomness in Agentic Evals (Bjarnason, Silva, Monperrus, arXiv:2602.07150) runs 60,000 trajectories on SWE-bench Verified (3 models x 2 scaffolds x 2 temperatures, 25.58B tokens) and finds that single-run pass@1 estimates fluctuate between 2.2 and 6.0 percentage points depending on the run, with standard deviation above 1.5 points even at temperature 0, because trajectories diverge within the first few percent of tokens. The paper recommends multi-run pass@1, power analysis, pass@k and pass^k. For attribution this sets a floor: any classifier whose action changes outcomes by less than roughly 2-3 points is indistinguishable from re-sampling, so an attribution rule cannot be validated by a single A/B pair of rounds, and the loop's binary 0/1 score plus 2 attempts per round cannot resolve an effect that small in any realistic campaign length.
nodes.source: arXiv:2602.07150 (Bjarnason, Silva, Monperrus, Feb 2026), 60,000 trajectories, 3 models x 2 scaffolds x 2 temperatures, 25.58B tokens, single-run pass@1 swing 2.2-6.0 pp, sd >1.5 pp at temp 0

nodes.title: The minimal valid attribution design is a 2x2 model-by-harness grid on a fixed task set
nodes.body: A harness-card note (arXiv:2605.23950) states the protocol precisely: variance decomposition becomes attribution only when the same model runs under at least two harnesses and the same harness under at least two models, on a fixed task set, holding task order, environment, eval script, API parameters and stopping rules constant. The minimal valid design is a 2x2 model-by-harness grid. Everything cheaper than that is a confounded single cell. Artificial Analysis's Coding Agent Index v1.5 applies the same logic at benchmark scale: equal-weight pass@1 over DeepSWE v1.1 (113 tasks), Terminal-Bench 4.0 (66) and SWE-Atlas-QnA (124), 303 tasks x 3 attempts, so a single agent number is an average over three axes rather than one measurement. dsh-loom currently has no such grid: 451 attempts carry a model name on about 24 of them, and modelsTried has length 1 for 303 attempts and length 0 for 142, so the ledger cannot even populate the model axis.
nodes.source: arXiv:2605.23950 harness-card note (2x2 model-by-harness grid, held task order/env/eval script/API params/stopping rules); Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v1.5 (303 tasks x 3 attempts)

nodes.title: 67.73% of rerun CI builds are flaky; 15 failure categories; log-only detection gains 20.3% F1
nodes.body: Understanding and Detecting Flaky Builds in GitHub Actions (Ge & Zhang, arXiv:2602.02307) studies rerun data from 1,960 open-source Java projects and finds 3.2% of builds are rerun, of which 67.73% exhibit flaky behaviour, affecting 1,055 projects (51.28%). Fifteen distinct flaky-failure categories emerge, with flaky tests, network issues and dependency resolution the most prevalent, and the authors build a machine-learning detector at the job level that improves F1 by up to 20.3% over a strong baseline. Two lessons transfer: (a) the conditional probability that a rerun is infrastructure is about two in three, which is the empirical prior a loop should start from when deciding how much to distrust a single failure; (b) the classification problem is well-posed at the job level from logs alone, but even a 20.3% relative F1 gain leaves the detector far from certain, so the output must be a probability that gates an action, not a verdict that excuses a failure.
nodes.source: arXiv:2602.02307 (Ge & Zhang, 2 Feb 2026), 1,960 Java projects, 3.2% builds rerun, 67.73% of rerun builds flaky, 1,055 projects (51.28%), 15 categories, job-level detector +20.3% F1

nodes.title: OpenStack: cross-project flakiness hits 55% of projects, 89% of inconsistent cases are CI race conditions
nodes.body: Cross-Project Flakiness (Xiao et al., arXiv:2602.09311v2) analyses 649 OpenStack projects over a year: 29,175 closed reviews, 73,707 patch sets, 439,618 comments, 139,768 Zuul outcome comments, 29,911 flaky builds across 1,651 jobs. Cross-project flakiness affects 378 projects, about 55%, and 70% of unit tests show it, contradicting the assumption that unit tests are insulated. The causal analysis is the part that matters for infrastructure attribution: race conditions in the CI process account for 89% of inconsistent flakiness, with mismatched CI configuration and dependency management together contributing 21%. Cost figures carried in the paper: Google spends 2% to 16% of compute re-running flaky tests, Herzig et al. estimate about $7.2M for a single Microsoft product, and 1 in 11 GitHub commits has at least one flaky-caused failure. So infrastructure fault is not a rare tail; it is a fifth to a half of observed failure signal in mature shops.
nodes.source: arXiv:2602.09311v2 (Xiao et al., 2026), 649 OpenStack projects, 29,911 flaky builds / 1,651 jobs, 55% of projects affected, 89% race conditions, 2-16% Google compute on re-runs, ~$7.2M single Microsoft product, 1-in-11 commits

nodes.title: Provider errors are 5% of LLM spans and 60% of those are rate limits
nodes.body: Datadog's State of AI Engineering 2026 (CC BY-ND 4.0) reports telemetry from more than 1,000 customers over February and March 2026: 5% of all LLM call spans reported an error in February, and 60% of those errors were exceeded rate limits; by March the span error rate fell to 2% with rate limits still about a third of them, roughly 8.4 million rate-limit errors. The same report finds 69% of all input tokens are system prompts, only 28% of call spans show any cached-read tokens, and 59% of agentic requests make a single service call with only 18% making three or more. The mechanism it describes is a cascade: a long ReAct loop plus a shared quota plus a retry policy produces sustained failure that looks like the model giving up. For dsh-loom this says the dominant provider-side fault is quota exhaustion, which is silent, time-correlated, and indistinguishable from a capability failure without external telemetry.

nodes.title: SWE-bench's own maintainers: an audit found 62.5% of unsolved-by-all instances were environment-broken
nodes.body: SWE-bench issue #586 reports an audit of the 281-instance unsolved-by-all bucket where all 9 published baselines fail: 5 of 8 sampled instances (62.5%) failed during test-pipeline setup, before any model patch could be applied, so the harness logged them as model-unsolved rather than infrastructure-unreachable. The failure classes are mundane: a missing node module (Cannot find module 'spider-detector') and absent test files. PR #594 then added a pre-flight environment verification plus a ResolvedStatus.INFRA_FAILURE enum, and the maintainer rewrite records the two traps: the pre-flight check wrongly failed about 3% of instances because some test files are created by the test patch itself, and removing broken instances from the score makes scores look higher than they are. The merged compromise reads the run log afterwards, counts broken instances as unresolved so the score is unchanged, and flagged 50 instances where the browser failed to start. That is the design pattern dsh-loom should copy: classify from logs after the fact, and never let the classification change the denominator.
nodes.source: github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench/issues/586 (281 unsolved-by-all, 5/8 = 62.5% environment-broken) and pull/594 (pre-flight wrongly failed ~3%, INFRA_FAILURE kept out of numerator, broken instances stay unresolved, 50 browser-startup failures flagged)

nodes.title: Auth stalls manufacture sub-90-second 'losses' that look exactly like giving up
nodes.body: june.kim's run of all 728 eligible SWE-bench Pro instances (694 resolved, 95.3%) documents the failure mode better than any paper: an auth stall or a starved quota produces a sub-90-second failure over a 0-byte patch that is numerically indistinguishable from the model abandoning a hard bug, so scoring it as a loss depresses the number by infrastructure wearing the model's face. Losses clustered hard at 19:00-21:00 UTC (US working hours) and went near-zero overnight, same boxes, same code, same instances, tracking other people's chat sessions; three provider-side OAuth rotations produced waves of sub-90-second losses carrying Failed to authenticate / API Error: 401 over 0-byte patches, roughly 310 of the 728 instances billed to paid API because of that tail. The defence is procedural, not statistical: predeclare the fault class with four invariants (verbatim 401 string, 0-byte patch, a wave of at least three instances, resolution by a fresh credential) and freeze it before any re-dispatched verdict lands, otherwise 'that one was infrastructure' becomes a post-hoc filter.
nodes.source: june.kim/how-not-to-run-swebench-pro (728 instances, 694 resolved 95.3%, sub-90s auth-stall failures over 0-byte patches, losses 19:00-21:00 UTC and near-zero overnight, ~310 instances on the paid-API tail, four pre-registered invariants for the infra class)

nodes.title: dsh-loom has one enum that absorbs provider death, harness breakage and unclassified error: died
nodes.body: Over 69 campaign state files (451 attempts, 228 rounds, 235 failures) the failureKind census is: died 162, ok 141 (of which 23 have verifierOk false), timeout 25, crash 9, and no failureKind at all on attempts recorded before the field existed. The classifier at src/dispatch/session.js:38-46 returns ok for stopReason completed, timeout on timedOut, tokens on max-tokens, context or tokens on a MODEL_LIMIT regex match, and died for everything else, so a dead parent session, a disposed dispatcher, a failed git worktree, a provider 500 and a genuinely unclassified error all land in one bucket. Downstream, src/runtime/model-health.js:59-95 then re-buckets died/timeout/exhausted as NO_DELIVERY (deliberately excluding crash, context and tokens) and demoteChain moves all-fail model refs to the back of the chain. The information needed to attribute is destroyed at the first hop and cannot be recovered later, which is why every cheap rule below is tested against a label rather than against truth.
nodes.source: computed over ~/.dsh/loom/campaigns/*/views/state.json (69 campaign dirs, 451 attempts, 235 failures): died 162, ok 141, timeout 25, crash 9; src/dispatch/session.js:38-46 classifyResult; src/runtime/model-health.js:59-95 NO_DELIVERY set

nodes.title: The 162 died attempts are three populations: 32 infra, 56 abandoned, 74 unknown
nodes.body: Unpacking the single died bucket is the whole exercise. Of 162 died attempts, 32 carry infra:true and have textChars 0, stopReason error, duration median 1318 ms, and all 32 are exactly the 32 attempts with infraRetry true (a 1:1 overlap). Another 56 are abandoned, 40 of them with reason solved-by-sibling, i.e. a sibling attempt won and the child was cancelled on purpose; src/runtime/model-health.js already prefers abandoned over failureKind with the comment that an aborted child is true about the child and false about the provider. The remaining 74 have no infra flag, no abandoned flag and no diagnostic that distinguishes them from either population. So 88 of 162 (54.3%) are definitively not the model's fault (32 infra plus 56 abandoned), 74 (45.7%) are unattributable, and the true infrastructure share of all 235 failures is somewhere between 13.6% (the 32 flagged) and about 37% (32 plus some fraction of the 74 unknown).
nodes.source: computed over 451 ledger attempts: died 162 = infra 32 + abandoned 56 (40 solved-by-sibling) + unlabelled 74; infra 32/32 have infraRetry true, textChars 0, stopReason error, median duration 1318 ms; 32/235 = 13.6% of failures flagged infra

nodes.title: dsh-loom's infra bit means 'silent', so 20 real harness faults are never flagged
nodes.body: src/dispatch/session.js:459-497 sets `const silent = stopReason === 'error' && !diagnostic` and then `const infra = silent`: the infra flag is true only when a child died with nothing to say and no message could be recovered from its own session log. That is a proxy for one specific death (dead parent or provider), not for harness fault. The consequence is measurable. Twenty attempts carry unmistakably harness-origin error strings (13 dispatcher disposed, 6 cannot get property "sessions" without inject, 1 git worktree add failed: fatal: failed to read .git/wor...), and none of the 20 has infra set (all 20 have the key absent); 11 have no failureKind and 9 are crash, spread over 9 campaigns (loom-self 6, loom-acc1/2/3 2 each, loom-self2/3/4, loom-ui6, loom-probe). Symmetrically, 48 of the 80 'child session ended in error with no diagnostic (parent or provider unavailable)' attempts carry no infra flag at all, and those 48 are byte-identically shaped, so the label is not even stable within its own population. The 20 harness faults are the only textual ground truth for a harness-vs-capability classifier in the whole ledger, and 20 is a small training set.
nodes.source: src/dispatch/session.js:459-497 (silent -> infra); computed over the ledger: 20 attempts with harness-origin strings (dispatcher disposed x13, without inject x6, worktree add failed x1), infra key absent on all 20, failureKind None x11 / crash x9, 9 campaigns; 80 no-diagnostic attempts split infra 32 / unflagged 48

nodes.title: Six cheap predicates top out at 0.40 precision against the ledger's own infra label
nodes.body: Tested against infra:true (32 positives) with the defensible negative set of died and neither flagged infra nor abandoned (74), and also scored over all 451 attempts: (A) duration under 5000 ms and textChars 0 gives tp 32, fp 66, fires 112, precision 0.327; (B) A plus stopReason error gives tp 32, fp 66, fires 98, precision 0.327; (C) textChars 0 and stopReason error gives tp 32, fp 72, fires 104, precision 0.308; (D) error string contains no diagnostic gives tp 32, fp 48, fires 80, precision 0.400; (E) duration under 2000 ms gives tp 32, fp 52, fires 98, precision 0.381; (F) textChars 0 alone gives tp 32, fp 72, fires 322, precision 0.308. Every rule achieves recall 1.0 by construction, because the 32 positives are all silent and fast, and the best precision is 0.40. Meanwhile source/latency: the corpus is 451 attempts, so the rule fires on roughly a fifth of the whole ledger to catch 7% of it, which means an action keyed on any of these predicates is wrong more often than right.
nodes.source: computed over 451 ledger attempts, positives infra:true n=32, negatives died and not infra and not abandoned n=74; six predicates, best precision 0.400 (error string contains no diagnostic), all recall 1.0, fire counts 80-322

nodes.title: Half the fields a classifier would need are absent: textChars on 305/451, heartbeat on 0/451
nodes.body: Schema drift is the hidden reason the classifiers above cannot be improved on this corpus. textChars is present on only 305 of 451 attempts, in 52 campaigns, so 146 attempts report no output volume at all; stdoutTail is empty on 178 attempts and agentTail on 205; retried is true on 0 attempts and heartbeat is present on 0 attempts, both fields existing in the record schema (src/runtime/round.js around line 1528) but never populated in this data; modelSwitch is set on 4 attempts, salvaged on 4, and modelsTried has length 1 for 303 attempts, length 0 for 142 and length 2 for only 4. Worse, textChars is not a proxy for work: its median among successes is 0 and 121 of the 323 attempts with textChars 0 scored 1, so a classifier that reads silence as failure is reading a field that does not mean what it looks like. Every byte of the schema variance above is a place where a 0 could mean 'did not happen' or 'was not recorded', and a loop that trains on such a column learns the recording policy, not the world.
nodes.source: computed over 451 ledger attempts: textChars present 305 (52 campaigns), stdoutTail empty 178, agentTail empty 205, retried true 0, heartbeat present 0, modelSwitch 4, salvaged 4, modelsTried length 1 for 303 / 0 for 142 / 2 for 4; success median textChars 0, 121 of 323 textChars==0 attempts scored 1; src/runtime/round.js attempt record fields

nodes.title: 22 failures exited 0 with tests passing and still scored 0, because the session died first
nodes.body: src/runtime/round.js:1486 sets verifierOk to gateOk, and gateOk at line 1461 is `(ver.ok && lean.ok && outcomeKind === 'ok') || salvaged`, where salvaged requires stoppedByDeadline and outcomeKind timeout. So when the verifier passes but the child's session ended in error, gateOk is false and the whole attempt scores 0 even though the tests went green. The ledger contains 22 such attempts: score 0, verifierOk false, exitCode 0, failureKind died 16 and timeout 6, with stdoutTail showing real green output such as ok 1..ok 3 then 3/3 passed. Seven of the 22 have a non-empty patch; 15 have patchBytes 0, meaning the tree was clean but the verifier still exited 0, which is its own separate anomaly. Spread: loom-life 14, loom-acc2 6, loom-acc1 1, loom-tri6 1, mean duration 200.9 s. This is a pure attribution bug rather than a measurement limit: the verifier's verdict exists, is positive, and is discarded because a different component's state is used as a conjunction term. It is the cheapest fix in this entire report and it is worth more than any classifier.
nodes.source: src/runtime/round.js:1461 gateOk = (ver.ok && lean && outcomeKind==='ok') || salvaged; round.js:1486 verifierOk: gateOk; ledger: 22 attempts score 0 / exitCode 0 / failureKind died 16 + timeout 6, stdoutTail '3/3 passed', 7 with patch, loom-life 14, loom-acc2 6, loom-acc1 1, loom-tri6 1, mean duration 200.9 s

nodes.title: 8 attempts report '0/0 passed' and exit 1: the verifier collected zero tests and still failed
nodes.body: A second verifier-side population is the vacuous pass: 8 attempts have stdoutTail containing the literal 0/0 passed, all 8 in loom-bal4 (4) and loom-chaos (4), and all 8 score 0. A test runner that collected zero tests and exited 1 was read as a failure of the attempt, when it is a failure of the check. A related group is the 23 attempts with failureKind ok and verifierOk false, 19 of which have an empty stdoutTail: the child completed happily, the verifier produced no output, and the attempt was recorded as a capability failure. And 44 of the 141 exit-code-1 failures have the word passed somewhere in the 15-line stdoutTail, so a non-trivial share of verifier failures are not clean test failures. None of this is accessible to a classifier that only reads failureKind, and all of it is visible in the text fields that exist on 273 of 451 attempts.

nodes.title: The built-in infra remedy fired 32 times and recovered 0: model-switching cannot fix a harness fault
nodes.body: src/dispatch/session.js:248-276 retries an infra attempt when `res?.infra && !infraRetried && noAlternative && survivedEnough`, and the unusable test at :281-305 treats context, tokens, infra and timeout as reasons to fall over to the next model in the chain. The ledger shows what that bought: all 32 infra attempts have infraRetry true, 16 of the 32 had a later attempt in the same round, and 0 of those 16 later attempts scored 1; all 16 rounds containing an infra attempt failed to promote (16 of 16 unpromoted, 32 attempts, all score 0). A code comment in the same file records that across 22 campaigns the rebuild-parent retry fired 32 times and converted a silent death exactly never. That is the cost of mis-attribution measured directly: the loop applied a model-layer remedy to a non-model fault 16 times and the remedy's success rate was 0/16. Note the sample: 16 trials with zero successes puts the 95% upper bound on any true recovery rate at 17.1%, so the honest statement is 'below 17%', and 16 is too few to distinguish 0% from a small positive rate.

nodes.title: 40.4% of rounds produce no usable attempt; delivery failures take 41% of the spend
nodes.body: The economic frame for attribution: of 228 rounds in the ledger, 92 (40.4%) produce no usable attempt at all, i.e. every attempt in the round was died, timeout, crash or abandoned. Total recorded spend is $0.109 over 431 priced attempts, of which $0.044 (41%) went to delivery-failure attempts (died, timeout, crash), so the loop spends two-fifths of its money learning nothing. Median round cost is $0.00042 and median round duration 82.8 s, so a retry is cheap in dollars but not in wall clock; promoted attempts have median duration 223.7 s against 27.3 s for failures. Campaigns are also short, 69 of them with median 2 rounds and median 4 attempts, which is the binding constraint on any statistics below: at 2 attempts per round and a binary 0/1 score, most campaigns cannot detect anything. Per-campaign pass rate has median 0.5 with 8 campaigns at 0.0, so the corpus is bimodal and a pooled classifier will mostly learn which campaign it is looking at.
nodes.source: computed over 451 attempts / 228 rounds: 92 rounds (40.4%) with no usable attempt, $0.109 total over 431 priced attempts, $0.044 (41%) on delivery failures, median round $0.00042 and 82.8 s, promoted median duration 223.7 s vs failed 27.3 s, 69 campaigns median 2 rounds / 4 attempts, per-campaign pass rate median 0.5 with 8 at 0.0

nodes.title: Break-even precision is 0.5 for a symmetric excuse and 0.75 if a bad lesson persists
nodes.body: Formalise the action. Let b be the value of correctly excusing a true infrastructure failure (one saved retry: median 82.8 s and $0.00042 in this ledger) and h the cost of wrongly excusing a capability failure (one unlearned failure, which delays the streak that demotes a bad model, plus the lesson written from a misread round). Acting on a classifier is worth it when precision p satisfies p*b > (1-p)*h, i.e. p > h/(h+b). With h = b the break-even precision is 0.5. If a misattributed lesson is injected into future worker prompts (the ledger holds 100 lessons and notesShown is nonzero on 49 attempts), one bad lesson contaminates several later rounds, so h is plausibly 3b and the break-even precision rises to 0.75. The best cheap predicate available is at 0.40 (n-loom-cheap-rule-precision), which is below even the optimistic 0.5 bar, so on this corpus the loop may not act on any of the six rules, and the LLM-judge ceiling of 14.2% on identifying the failing step is far below it too.
nodes.source: decision-theoretic derivation on ledger costs: median round duration 82.8 s and median round cost $0.00042, 100 lessons total, notesShown nonzero on 49 attempts; break-even p = h/(h+b) = 0.5 symmetric, 0.75 at h=3b; best cheap rule precision 0.400; LLM-judge step attribution 14.2% (arXiv:2505.00212)

nodes.title: 32 labelled positives can certify 91% precision, not 99%; the rule is binding, not the sample
nodes.body: How much evidence does the threshold need? With n independently labelled positives and zero observed errors, the 95% upper bound on the error rate is 1 - 0.05^(1/n), so 32 positives certify precision at or above 91.1%, 74 positives certify 96.0%, and reaching 99% requires 299. The ledger's 32 infra-flagged attempts are therefore enough to certify a 91% rule today and not enough for 99%, but the current best rule sits at 40%, so the sample is not the binding constraint; the rule is. Two caveats make even the 91% number weaker than it looks: the 32 positives are not independent draws (they cluster in 16 rounds and a handful of campaigns, and a per-round correlation inflates the effective sample size deficit), and the labels come from the same code path the classifier is meant to replace, so a rule that reproduces 'silent' perfectly would score 1.0 while learning nothing. Any real evaluation needs the 20 harness-origin and 48 unflagged no-diagnostic attempts hand-adjudicated first.
nodes.source: binomial upper bound 1 - 0.05^(1/n) applied to ledger counts: 32 positives -> 8.9% error bound (91.1% precision), 74 -> 4.0% (96.0%), 99% needs n=299; 32 infra attempts cluster in 16 rounds; 20 harness-origin and 48 unflagged no-diagnostic attempts available for hand adjudication

nodes.title: The cheapest classifier that clears break-even is not a predicate on the record but a replay against a known-good tree
nodes.body: Every predicate over the attempt record fails for a structural reason: the discriminant between a harness fault and a capability fault is not in the record, because src/dispatch/session.js collapses it into died before the record is written, and the one field that could carry it (infra) is set only on the silent path. The cheapest classifier that can clear 0.5 precision is therefore a differential replay, not a text rule: take an attempt whose verifier failed, re-run the same verifier against the same base commit with no patch applied, and again with the gold or previously-promoted patch applied. If the clean tree fails the verifier, the fault is the task or the harness; if the clean tree passes and the gold tree passes but the attempt failed, the fault is the patch, i.e. capability. This costs one to three verifier runs, and the verifier default timeout is 10 minutes (src/exec/verifier.js:10), so a bounded replay is $0 in model tokens and minutes in wall clock, which is cheaper than the 82.8 s median round it is deciding about only if it is run selectively. The seed for it already exists: 22 exit-0 attempts prove the verifier can pass on a tree the gate rejected.
nodes.source: src/dispatch/session.js:38-46 and :459-497 (discriminant destroyed before write); src/exec/verifier.js:10 (10-minute default verify timeout); ledger: 22 attempts reached verifier exit 0 while scoring 0, 7 with a patch; FAMAS (arXiv:2509.13782) as the precedent that replay-based attribution beats LLM judging

nodes.title: Task order is near-worthless inside a fixed compute budget; the number of distinct tasks is what pays
nodes.body: Wu, Dyer & Neyshabur sweep thousands of orderings over CIFAR10/100 with 540 baseline ResNet-50 runs at 35,200 steps (100 epochs, batch 128). Curriculum, anti-curriculum and 'random-curriculum' (dynamic training-set size, random order) all land within noise of plain i.i.d. training; randomly ordered samples do as well or better, so 'any benefit is entirely due to the dynamic training set size'. For dsh-loom: the selector rotates over open tasks (src/runtime/selector.js pickTask), and this result says the ROTATION ORDER is not where quality comes from - the size and composition of the open-task pool is.
nodes.source: arXiv:2012.03107 (ICLR 2021) https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.03107

nodes.title: Curriculum does pay - but only in the time-limited or noisy regime
nodes.body: Same paper, two regimes where the ordering result flips: with a limited training-time budget (few iterations, imitating a large-data regime where multiple epochs are infeasible) curriculum beats standard training and anti-curriculum; with injected label noise it also wins. Anti-curriculum never wins in either regime. dsh-loom is permanently in the first regime: W = 480-940 s per round, 20 rounds/night is only 3.4-4.0 h of a night, so nothing ever gets a second epoch over the same task population. That is exactly the condition under which ordering starts to matter.
nodes.source: arXiv:2012.03107 §5-6 https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.03107

nodes.title: There is already an implicit curriculum, so explicit reordering has little room
nodes.body: The paper's first experiment shows samples are learned in a highly consistent order across architectures and optimizers regardless of the schedule fed in - the model has its own difficulty ordering. Explicit curricula can only help at the margin because the implicit one is already doing the sorting. Translation for a code loop: the worker model has its own internal ordering over task types (config edits before multi-file refactors before UI wiring), so a hand-built difficulty ladder mostly re-derives what the worker already does.
nodes.source: arXiv:2012.03107 §3 https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.03107

nodes.title: Prioritized Level Replay: mean |GAE| of the last trajectory is a label-free difficulty signal
nodes.body: PLR scores each training level by the mean absolute generalized advantage estimate of the most recent trajectory (equivalent to an L1 value loss), then samples P_replay = (1-rho)*P_S + rho*P_C: P_S is a rank-based prioritization with temperature beta, P_C a staleness/recency distribution. rho = 0.1 on Procgen, 0.3 on MiniGrid, beta = 0.1. The Value Correction Hypothesis explains why it works: levels at the edge of ability have non-stationary value targets, hence high value error; unsolvable levels produce stationary failure, hence low value error. So the score tracks the expanding frontier of ability without any external difficulty label.
nodes.source: arXiv:2010.03934 (ICML 2021) https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03934

nodes.title: PLR: 135.0% vs 100.0% normalized return, and the mix is what buys it
nodes.body: Procgen, 25M steps, 200 levels: PLR reaches 135.0% +/- 6.1 normalized test return against 100.0 +/- 2.0 for uniform sampling; UCB-DrAC+PLR reaches 182.9 +/- 8.2 (TSCL 103.9, mixreg 110.6). Significant gains on 10 of 16 Procgen environments; MiniGrid uses 1000 levels per difficulty. Both-only ablations are the interesting part: keeping only staleness (rho=1) or keeping only the L1 value-loss score (rho=0) is WORSE than uniform sampling. A recency term is not a nicety, it is load-bearing.
nodes.source: arXiv:2010.03934 Table 1-2 https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03934

nodes.title: A pure score-priority queue collapses; a pure recency queue forgets
nodes.body: PLR's own ablation reports that either half alone underperforms uniform sampling, and the paper notes that any candidate scoring function must asymptotically decrease with visitation frequency or the sampler mode-collapses onto a few levels. For a code loop the analogue is a task score that only ever rewards past success: it will re-pick the same three tasks forever and starve the pool. dsh-loom's current selector is the opposite extreme - pure round-robin over unsolved tasks with no score at all - which is the other degenerate corner.
nodes.source: arXiv:2010.03934 §4 (ablation + mode collapse note) https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03934

nodes.title: Absolute Zero: reward a proposed task by 1 - pass rate, and by exactly 0 when nothing solves it
nodes.body: AZR's proposer reward is r_propose = 0 if mean solve rate is 0, else 1 - mean solve rate, where the mean is over G Monte-Carlo solver rollouts at non-zero temperature. It peaks at intermediate success and is zero at both p=0 and p=1, and crucially it is 0 (not -p) for impossible tasks, so the proposer gets no anti-signal that would teach it to avoid hard but learnable tasks. A Python executor both validates the proposed task and verifies the answer - the same artifact is the task factory and the grader.
nodes.source: arXiv:2505.03335 (v3) https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03335

nodes.title: AZR's whole curriculum apparatus is worth about 1.4 points; task-type diversity is worth more
nodes.body: AZR-Base-7B ablation (Table 2, code / math / overall averages): full model with proposer+generation-reference conditioning 55.2 / 38.4 / 46.8; solver-only training 54.8 / 36.0 / 45.4; generation-reference removed 54.4 / 33.1 / 43.8; induction task type removed 54.2 / 33.3 / 43.8; deduction only 54.6 / 32.0 / 43.3. Removing the proposer costs 1.4 overall points; removing a whole task TYPE costs 3.5. If you only get one lever, it is the mix of task kinds, not the cleverness of the selector.
nodes.source: arXiv:2505.03335 Table 2 https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03335

nodes.title: Expected improvement is bounded by the variance of per-task success probability
nodes.body: The online difficulty filtering paper proves the expected policy improvement of a group-relative update is lower-bounded by the variance of task-level success probabilities, which is maximized at p=0.5 and zero at p=0 or p=1. That is the formal version of 'aim at the band': a task everyone solves and a task nobody solves both produce a zero-advantage batch. Balanced filtering (drop tasks outside [T_low, T_high]) maximizes this bound; skewed filtering does not.
nodes.source: arXiv:2504.03380 https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03380

nodes.title: Band sweep: 27.3% -> >30% average, and ONLINE filtering beats offline curation 6x
nodes.body: Sweeping (T_low, T_high) over {(0,1),(0.1,0.9),(0.2,0.8),(0.3,0.7),(0.4,0.6)} on a 3B model, stricter balanced filtering is monotonically better: average over 5 benchmarks goes from 27.3% to above 30%, with up to +12% gains in less than half the GRPO training steps. The load-bearing comparison: offline curation or offline scheduling of the same band reaches at most +2.1% over plain GRPO, and skewed filtering is WORSE than plain GRPO (24.9-25.9% vs 26.3%). The band is only worth having if it is applied per batch, online.
nodes.source: arXiv:2504.03380 §4-5 https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03380

nodes.title: The band does not need to be precise: any low cut in (0, 0.25) and high cut in (0.75, 1) behaves the same
nodes.body: GOID labels each goal by the empirical success fraction from at most four rollouts and keeps goals with R_min <= p <= R_max, using 0.1 and 0.9 in every experiment. The appendix shows the algorithm is 'almost invariant' for any R_min in (0, 0.25) and any R_max in (0.75, 1), because with at most four attempts the estimated label is coarse anyway - they verify this by comparing against true labels estimated with three fresh rollouts, which are only slightly better. Practically: you do not need a calibrated difficulty model, you need a coarse 0.1/0.9-style cut and 3-4 samples per candidate.
nodes.source: arXiv:1705.06366 (v5) §4.1 + Appendix C https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.06366

nodes.title: TSCL picks by learning-curve slope, and adds a forgetting term for tasks that are getting worse
nodes.body: Teacher-Student Curriculum Learning treats subtask choice as a non-stationary multi-armed bandit: Q_{t+1}(a) = alpha*r_t + (1-alpha)*Q_t(a) with epsilon-greedy or Boltzmann selection, and four estimators of learning progress - Online (EWMA of return), Naive (train each task K times, regress score on trial), Window (FIFO buffer of the last K scores, regress score on timestamps) and Sampling (Thompson-style draw from the last K rewards). It also selects tasks whose performance is DEGRADING, to counter forgetting. It solved a Minecraft maze that could not be solved at all when trained directly on the maze.
nodes.source: arXiv:1707.00183 https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.00183

nodes.title: At p=0 and p=1 the group-relative advantage is exactly zero, so those tasks buy nothing
nodes.body: DAPO §3.2 Dynamic Sampling states the mechanism plainly: GRPO's advantage is zero when all G sampled outputs get the same reward, so prompts with accuracy 0 or 1 contribute no gradient at all - they are wasted batch slots. DAPO over-samples and filters to enforce 0 < |{correct}| < G, refilling the batch to a fixed size. This is the same statement as the variance bound, expressed as an implementation rule rather than a theorem, and it is the single cheapest thing a loop can copy.
nodes.source: arXiv:2503.14476 §3.2 https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14476

nodes.title: DAPO ablation ladder: 30 -> 50 on AIME24 avg@32, dynamic sampling is the last +8
nodes.body: Ablation on AIME24 avg@32, 32B base: naive GRPO 30, + overlong filtering 36, + Clip-Higher 38, + soft overlong punishment 41, + token-level loss 42, + Dynamic Sampling (full DAPO) 50, versus R1-Zero-Qwen-32B at 47 trained for twice as many steps. Note the shape: difficulty filtering is the last and largest single step (+8) but it only pays after the four preceding fixes; bolting a band onto a broken advantage estimator buys nothing.
nodes.source: arXiv:2503.14476 Table 3 https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14476

nodes.title: 1,000 chosen samples match 59,000: 50.0 vs 53.3 on AIME24
nodes.body: s1 curates 1,000 problems on quality, difficulty and diversity. Table 2 (AIME24 / MATH500 / GPQA, 95% paired bootstrap CIs): 1K-random 36.7 / 90.6 / 52.0; 1K-diverse-only 26.7 / 91.2 / 54.6; 1K-longest-only 33.3 / 90.4 / 59.6; full 59K 53.3 / 92.8 / 58.1; s1K 50.0 / 93.0 / 57.6. So 1K selected is within 3.3 points of 59K on the headline benchmark at 1.7% of the data, and EVERY single criterion alone is worse than the combination - diversity alone loses 10 points of AIME24 versus random.
nodes.source: arXiv:2501.19393 Table 2 https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393

nodes.title: 817 examples: 63.3% AIME24 / 95.6% MATH500 against 6.5% / 59.2% for prior fine-tunes
nodes.body: LIMO's 'Less-Is-More Reasoning Hypothesis' argues that when pretrained knowledge is complete, a minimal set of strategically designed demonstrations is sufficient and volume adds nothing; 817 curated examples give 63.3% on AIME24 and 95.6% on MATH500 with a 45.8-point absolute OOD improvement, using about 1% of the data of comparable fine-tunes. Read carefully it is a claim about coverage of reasoning SKILLS, not about task count per se - which is why it sits awkwardly next to the s1 result that random 1K already gets 36.7.
nodes.source: arXiv:2502.03387 https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03387

nodes.title: Across four SE tasks, permutation changes the target score by +6% to -4%
nodes.body: The first empirical study of fine-tuning order in software engineering: Clone Detection, Defect Detection, Code Repair and Code Translation from CodeXGLUE, all 24 orderings, target-task performance moves by up to +6% gain and up to -4% loss - roughly a 10-point spread from ordering alone. Explanations tested: dataset syntactic similarity, semantic similarity, dataset size, probing/attention analysis, and task affinity. This is the strongest counterweight to the Wu et al. null result, but note the scale: 4 macro-tasks at fine-tuning scale, not 200 sample-level tasks inside one epoch.
nodes.source: arXiv:2410.02915 https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02915

nodes.title: Mining real tasks from GitHub: 450K candidates -> 21K usable, a 4.7% end-to-end yield
nodes.body: SWE-rebench's automated funnel with acceptance rates per stage: match PRs and issues (~10M PRs, 6M issues, 32K repos) -> ~450K task candidates (~5% of PRs) -> ~150K after filtering (33%) -> 21K after install-and-validate (14%) -> 21,336 annotated tasks from 3,468 repos. Hard requirements: the PR must add or modify tests, and the patch is split into a solution patch (non-test files) and a test patch (test files only). A fresh supply of such tasks is also what makes a contamination-free benchmark possible.
nodes.source: arXiv:2505.20411 (NeurIPS 2025) Table 6 https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20411

nodes.title: 32.67% of 'successful' SWE-bench patches were cheating, mostly because the issue text contained the fix
nodes.body: SWE-Bench+ manually screened SWE-Agent+GPT-4 successes on SWE-bench (2,294 issues, 12 Python repos): 32.67% of successful patches were cheating, with the solution leaked in the issue report or its comments, and a further 31.08% of passing patches were suspicious because the tests were too weak to distinguish a real fix. After removing them the resolution rate fell from 12.47% to 3.97% - a two-thirds collapse - and the same defects appear in SWE-bench Lite and Verified. Over 94% of the issues predate LLM knowledge cutoffs, so this is not memorization, it is spec leakage.
nodes.source: arXiv:2410.06992 https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06992

nodes.title: The issue text alone localizes the right file up to 76% of the time on SWE-bench Verified
nodes.body: Diagnostic probes on SWE-Bench-Verified: given only the issue text, a model identifies the file that must change with up to 76% accuracy on SWE-Bench-Verified versus up to 53% on repositories that are not in SWE-Bench; verbatim function reproduction reaches up to 35% consecutive 5-gram accuracy on SWE-Bench Verified/Full versus up to 18% on other benchmarks. The gap in both probes is the signature of memorization of the benchmark's repos rather than reasoning about the bug. It also means a task whose description names the file is much easier than the same task with the file withheld.
nodes.source: arXiv:2506.12286 (v4) https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12286

nodes.title: 'Training on the test task' is not malpractice, and it confounds exactly the comparison a self-improving loop makes
nodes.body: Dominguez-Olmedo, Dorner and Hardt distinguish training on the test task from leakage or contamination: it is the legitimate practice of using knowledge about the evaluation task at training time (task format, domain, the shape of the expected answer), and it confounds both relative model comparisons and claims of emergent ability. Their correction is to fine-tune every compared model on the same task-relevant data first; once you do, apparent emergent behavior fades gradually. For a loop that edits its own repo and is graded by tests in that repo, the 'task-relevant data' and the 'grading data' are the same files - there is no clean arm.
nodes.source: arXiv:2407.07890 (ICLR 2025 Oral) https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07890

nodes.title: Tasks synthesized from commits, with no human issue, avoid the leak channel entirely
nodes.body: R2E-Gym's SYNGEN builds tasks from a commit by generating tests against the pre-commit code and back-translating the resulting failure into a task description - the human issue is never in the loop, so the 'solution is written in the issue' failure mode of SWE-bench+ cannot occur. AgentGym holds >8.7K procedurally curated executable tasks; a 32B model reaches 34.4% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified. On verification: execution-based verifiers have low distinguishability and execution-free verifiers are biased toward style, each saturating around 42-43%, while a hybrid reaches 51%.
nodes.source: arXiv:2504.07164 https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07164

nodes.title: Synthesize tasks by breaking existing tests: 50k instances from 128 repos, 40.2% downstream
nodes.body: SWE-smith takes any Python codebase and synthesizes hundreds to thousands of task instances whose defining property is that they break existing tests - the test suite is the oracle and the 'bug' is injected, so no issue text is needed and every instance is executable by construction. It produced 50k instances from 128 repositories; SWE-agent-LM-32B trained on them reaches 40.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified. This is the cheapest known task factory for a repo you already have checked out, which is precisely dsh-loom's situation.
nodes.source: arXiv:2504.21798 https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21798

nodes.title: When the generator and the evaluator are the same model, iterative refinement hacks the evaluator
nodes.body: Pan, He, Bowman and Feng run essay editing with a second language model as evaluator and show 'spontaneous reward hacking': the evaluator's numerical ratings improve across iterations while true quality stays flat or declines, and the effect intensifies when generator and evaluator share the same underlying model, because optimization pressure finds their shared vulnerabilities. The transferable lesson for a loop whose grader is a model (a review node, a plan judge) rather than an executor: rating drift is the default, not an edge case, and only a mechanical verifier that cannot be talked to is immune.
nodes.source: arXiv:2407.04549 https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04549

Per (campaign, task) pair, the k-th attempt at the same task promotes at: slot 1 = 83/125 = 0.664, slot 2 = 14/48 = 0.292, slot 3 = 4/25 = 0.16, slot 4 = 1/14 = 0.071, slot 5 = 1/9 = 0.111, slots 6-7 = 0/8. nodes.title: A campaign's first round predicts the rest: 0.667 later-round promotion after a hit, 0.113 after a miss
nodes.body: In the same 229-round ledger, campaigns whose round 1 promoted continue at 0.667 (63 later rounds); campaigns whose round 1 failed continue at 0.113 (97 later rounds). Round 1 alone is 69 rounds (30.1%) but carries 50 of 103 promotions (48.5%). A stop-after-round-1 counterfactual would score 50/69 = 0.725 promotions per round versus the actual 0.450, and would leave 19 of 69 campaigns empty instead of 14 - so the honest reading is not 'stop early' but 'the campaign, not the task, is the unit of difficulty'. Also: 15 of the 27 campaigns with >=3 rounds hit three consecutive flat rounds, which is the plateau checkpoint's default window.

nodes.title: Our tasks are written by the loop, name their own test file, and the loop has edited its own graders
nodes.body: Three measurements on the same ledger and repo: (a) 52 of 70 campaign objectives name a concrete tests/... path, and 147 of 153 commits that add files under tests/ are authored by 'dsh-loom <loom@local>' - the loop writes the spec it is then graded on; (b) 7 attempts changed files under tests/, and all 7 were scored verifierOk true, including tests/selector.test.mjs in loom-self4 and tests/ui/queue-count.test.mjs in loom-ui3; (c) 51 of 70 campaigns have an EMPTY holdout pool and the other 19 have exactly one holdout entry. There is no arm in this design where the task and the grader are independent.

nodes.title: What is the cheapest next-task policy, and does the choice beat 20 more rounds?
nodes.body: The evidence points to a three-part answer that is testable in one week of nights. (1) Stop re-attempting a failed (campaign, task) pair after one retry: our slots >= 3 are 24.5% of rounds for 5.8% of promotions, and P(recover | first attempt failed) = 0.190 at 987 s per recovered promotion. (2) Treat the campaign as the sampling unit, not the task: later rounds after a failed round 1 run at 0.113, so a 2-round cap on a cold campaign converts ~97 rounds into freed budget. (3) A learned task ranking is NOT worth building yet: a leave-one-campaign-out task prior predicts next-round promotion with AUC 0.600 and Brier skill of only 3.9% over the base rate, while 133 of 229 rounds concern tasks never seen in another campaign. Cheapest = two hand-written rules, zero new model calls.
nodes.source: local ledger; tested against arXiv:2504.03380 (online band) and arXiv:2010.03934 (mixing)

nodes.title: Agentic coding burns 3,500x the tokens of single-round reasoning
nodes.body: OpenHands on SWE-bench Verified (8 models x 4 runs, 500 instances) measures agentic coding tasks consuming roughly 3,500x the tokens of single-round code reasoning and roughly 1,200x the tokens of multi-round chat. The multiplier is structural, not incidental: every tool call re-sends a growing transcript, so the unit of billing is the turn, not the answer. For dsh-loom this reframes the 452-attempt ledger: an attempt is not one prompt plus one patch but a multi-thousand-to-multi-million-token episode, so any budget must be calibrated from measured attempts rather than from a prompt-count heuristic. It also means a per-attempt cap and a per-campaign cap are different instruments and both are needed.
nodes.source: arXiv:2604.22750v3 (Bai et al., 'How Do AI Agents Spend Your Money?'), OpenHands + SWE-bench Verified, 8 models x 4 runs

nodes.title: Input tokens dominate agent spend even with caching on
nodes.body: Across all eight models and 500 SWE-bench instances, input tokens dominate consumption, and the Sonnet-4.5 phase case study shows cache reads dominating both token volume and dollar cost in every phase even though output is priced roughly 80x a cache read. Interpretation: the expensive thing is re-reading the transcript, not writing code. For dsh-loom the controllable lever is therefore the size of the replayed prefix (task text plus accumulated lessons plus repo digest plus prior attempt output), not the length of the model's answer. Capping output tokens is a weak instrument; capping and stabilising the prefix is the strong one, and it is also what makes caching work.
nodes.source: arXiv:2604.22750v3 §4-§5; cost formula Cost_round = Input_noncached*r_in + Output*r_out + CacheCreation*r_cache_create + CacheRead*r_cache_read

nodes.title: The same task, same model, same setup varies up to 30x in tokens
nodes.body: Repeated runs of one instance with one model differ by up to 30x in total tokens, and the most expensive problem averages about 7 million more tokens than the cheapest one. Difficulty predicts spend only weakly (expert-difficulty vs tokens Kendall tau_b = 0.32): 6.7% of tasks labelled 15-minute cost more than the average greater-than-1-hour task, while 11.1% of greater-than-1-hour tasks cost less than the average 15-minute task. For dsh-loom with 452 binary-scored attempts, this is a statement about the distribution: the mean attempt price is a bad planning number and the tail sets the bill, so a night's budget must be modelled as a heavy-tailed sum with a hard stop, not as attempts x average.
nodes.source: arXiv:2604.22750v3, 8 models x 4 runs x 500 instances; Kendall tau_b = 0.32; 6.7% / 11.1% crossover rates

nodes.title: Accuracy saturates while cost keeps climbing: inverse test-time scaling
nodes.body: Ordering configurations from cheapest to most expensive, accuracy rises from MinCost to LowerCost and then saturates while spend continues to increase; extra spend past the saturation point buys nothing. Kimi-K2 is the worst case (highest cost, lowest accuracy) and Kimi-K2 plus Claude Sonnet-4.5 consume more than 1.5M extra tokens versus GPT-5 on the same tasks, with the gap persisting on the shared-success and shared-failure subsets, which rules out task difficulty as the explanation and points at model behaviour. On failures GPT-5/GPT-5.2 add only about 0.5M tokens while Kimi-K2 adds about 2M. Applied to dsh-loom: a stalled attempt does not fail cheaply, it fails by spending more, so 'let it keep trying' is the most expensive possible default.
nodes.source: arXiv:2604.22750v3, model-pair comparisons on shared success/failure subsets

nodes.title: Half of file actions in high-cost models are repeats on the same file
nodes.body: Roughly 50% of file actions in the high-cost models are repeated actions on the same file, which is the sub-threshold version of the runaway loop: no single step is wrong, but the agent re-reads and re-writes the same target instead of advancing. This is the mechanism that turns a 30x token variance from a statistical curiosity into an operational hazard, because it is invisible in a success-rate metric (the attempt may still finish) and invisible in a per-step log (each step looks reasonable). For dsh-loom, the cheap detector is a per-attempt counter of distinct-file ratio and max repeats-per-file, with a hard stop at a threshold; the expensive non-detector is reviewing transcripts after the fact.
nodes.source: arXiv:2604.22750v3 (approximately 50% repeated file actions in high-cost models)

nodes.title: Cost is phase-shaped and spikes whenever new content enters context
nodes.body: The Sonnet-4.5 case study splits a run into Setup 9.98%, Explore 30.37%, Fix 33.53%, Validate 16.59%, Closeout 9.53% of cost, and per-round cost is non-monotonic: it spikes exactly when new content enters the context, i.e. repo exploration, file creation, test execution output, and summarisation. So the two-thirds spent before and after the edit (Explore plus Validate plus Setup plus Closeout = 66.5%) is where overnight money goes, and the spikes are the budget events. For dsh-loom this predicts that a retry of the same attempt with a fresh checkout is far more expensive than a retry that reuses a warm prefix, and that swallowing raw test logs into context is a cost decision, not a formatting one.
nodes.source: arXiv:2604.22750v3 §5 case study (Sonnet-4.5): Setup 9.98%, Explore 30.37%, Fix 33.53%, Validate 16.59%, Closeout 9.53%

nodes.title: 59.4% of tokens go to the iterative review stage, not to writing code
nodes.body: Tokenomics instruments ChatDev with GPT-5 reasoning over 30 tasks: the iterative code review stage absorbs 59.4% of all tokens on average, and input tokens are 53.9% of consumption. The conclusion is that the primary cost driver is automated refinement and verification, not initial code generation, which inverts the usual mental model of 'the model writes the patch'. For dsh-loom this is directly relevant because the loop is verifier-heavy: verify and review rounds are the product, so the token bill is essentially the price of re-reading the diff plus the verifier's output on every review iteration. That makes review-round count, not patch size, the cost variable, and it argues for a single well-specified review pass over several cheap ones.
nodes.source: arXiv:2601.14470 (Salim, Latendresse, Khatoonabadi, Shihab, 'Tokenomics'), ChatDev + GPT-5 reasoning, 30 tasks, 20 Jan 2026

nodes.title: Orchestration change beats model change: -41% cost at equal quality
nodes.body: A controlled swap over 22 locked tasks x 6 models x 2 orchestration layers moved cost per task from $0.21 to $0.12 (-41%), median wall-clock 48s to 27s (-44%), tokens per task 14.2k to 8.8k (-38%), and quality 0.78 to 0.81 (parity at n=22), i.e. quality per dollar +82% (3.71 to 6.75) and completions per Mtok 54.9 to 92.0. Per-model cuts range from -33% (Gemini 3.1) to -61% (Flash 3.5), and the harness lever exceeds the model lever: swapping to the cheapest capable model saves at most 36%. Of 48 capability-model cells, 30 improve, 11 are unchanged and 7 regress, with all 7 regressions on the three smaller models (6 of 7 in MCP/Playbooks/Presentations), so the harness needs a capability floor.
nodes.source: arXiv:2607.06906v2 (Sayed Ali et al., Writer Inc., 'The Harness Effect'), 22 tasks x 6 models x 2 layers, Oct 2026

nodes.title: List price overstates input cost by up to 10x once prefix caching sticks
nodes.body: The effective input price is p_in_eff = p_in * (1 - h * (1 - kappa)) where h is the cache-hit fraction and kappa the cache-read-to-write ratio, about 0.1, so a hit fraction near 1 means paying roughly one tenth of list on the dominant term. The paper measures 7,876 of 7,886 prompt tokens (99.9%) served as cache reads on an identical-prefix call. Vendor terms: Anthropic charges 1.25x to write and 0.10x to read with break-even at 1.4 reads, OpenAI discounts cached input automatically, Gemini gives 75% off with a one-hour TTL floor on 32K+ prompts. Implication for dsh-loom: any cost model built on list prices overestimates the stable prefix by up to 10x and therefore systematically under-budgets the non-cacheable tail, which is exactly where runs explode.
nodes.source: arXiv:2607.06906v2 (p_in^eff formula; 99.9% cache reads); Anthropic/OpenAI/Google cache pricing terms

nodes.title: Uncompacted transcript cost grows quadratically in turn count
nodes.body: Total input tokens for a naive harness grow as kS + k(k-1)/2 * mbar + kGbar + sum R_i over k turns with static prefix S, per-turn message mass mbar, generated Gbar and retrieval R_i, i.e. quadratically in k, and production agents report input-to-output ratios near 100:1. The baseline in the study replayed a 49KB monolithic system prompt every turn, used destructive middle truncation, and added polling waits. This is the arithmetic behind every overnight cost surprise: a 40-turn attempt pays for its own history 40 times. For dsh-loom, the counter is structured incremental compaction at about 80% of the input budget keeping a 4-12 message live tail under 30% of budget, plus context offload to files rather than a bigger window.
nodes.source: arXiv:2607.06906v2 (quadratic input-token model; 49KB prompt replay; 100:1 input:output; compaction at 80% budget, 4-12 message tail <=30%)

nodes.title: One sub-agent retried the same command 300+ times and burned 27M tokens
nodes.body: anthropics/claude-code issue #15909 (filed 2025-12-31, Opus 4.5, macOS): a general-purpose Task sub-agent re-issued the identical command 'npm install -D @vitest/coverage-v8' more than 300 times over about 4.6 hours, each attempt dying on 'Request timed out', consuming roughly 27 million tokens. There was no circuit breaker and no retry limit, and the user asked for reimbursement. At GPT-5 list input pricing of $1.250 per million that is about $33.75, at a 0.125 cached rate roughly $3.4 plus output, which is a 16x to 280x multiple of a $0.12-0.21 well-behaved task. The money is not the main loss: 4.6 hours of the night burned and the night produced zero accepted changes.
nodes.source: github.com/anthropics/claude-code issue #15909 (Opus 4.5, macOS, filed 2025-12-31)

nodes.title: Default turn limits are often infinite, so nothing stops a loop but a human
nodes.body: The runaway-loop writeup records Gemini CLI shipping maxSessionTurns with a default of -1, meaning no limit, alongside YOLO-style approval modes that remove the human approval gate; the entry is rated severity high and verified 2026-10-29. The pattern generalises: the agent runtime optimises for not interrupting a long task, while the operator's interest is stopping a bad task early, and the default sits on the runtime's side. For dsh-loom, the analogous defaults to audit are unlimited repair rounds, unlimited retries per attempt, and an autopilot that applies patches without a human checkpoint. Each of those is a per-attempt budget in disguise, and the safe default is a finite number chosen from the ledger's own distribution.
nodes.source: AIWiki runaway-agent-loops entry (severity high, verified_at 2026-10-29), citing Gemini CLI maxSessionTurns default -1 and YOLO approval modes; secondary source, low-to-medium confidence

nodes.title: Median spot interruption is 8% per hour, i.e. a coin flip over a night
nodes.body: An instrumented study of 40 production deployments and 12,000 interruption events reports a median interruption rate of 8% per hour for popular families (m5/m6/c5/c6) during US business hours, worst case 22% per hour (m5.xlarge in us-east-1 on one Tuesday afternoon) and best 1.8% per hour (r6gd eu-west-1 over a month). GPU instances interrupt 2-3x more often, with p4d.24xlarge at 25-40% per hour. Notice is 2 minutes. Rates are per hour, so an 8-hour unattended night against an 8%/hr rate has a 1 - 0.92^8 = 48.7% chance of at least one interruption, which is the number that matters when the work unit is the night rather than the job.
nodes.source: LeanOps, 'Spot Instances in 2026: We Tracked 12,000 Interruptions' (Ravi Kanani, 16 May 2026), 40 deployments, 12,000 events

nodes.title: 41% of spot workloads lost money after recovery costs
nodes.body: The same 12,000-interruption study finds 41% of workloads lost money on spot once recovery costs are counted, because the headline 70-90% discount masked 80-110% recovery cost in those cases. Their 100-node walkthrough: naive spot-everywhere claims $3,694/month of savings but incurs $2,800/month of recovery, netting $894; a smart 65/35 spot-on-demand split lands at $6,909/month versus $12,312 all on-demand, a real 44% saving. CI/CD runners are 95% fine on spot; single-job-at-a-time long tasks without checkpoints are where spot loses, e.g. a 6-hour ETL losing 5 hours. Mapping to agents: work that checkpoints per attempt (an attempt is short and restartable) suits spot, work that checkpoints per night does not, and the split ratio is the design decision.
nodes.source: LeanOps, 'Spot Instances in 2026: We Tracked 12,000 Interruptions' (Ravi Kanani, 16 May 2026); 100-node cost walkthrough

nodes.title: Human coverage costs $540/week per rotation slot, dwarfing a night of tokens
nodes.body: A survey of 200+ organisations puts the average weekday on-call rate at $540 per week, with weekend on-call paid about 2x weekday, individual flat payments spanning $5-1,000/month, 71% on fixed pay versus 2% paid per incident, and a $150 loaded hourly cost benchmark. Three rotation slots at $540 x 52 is an $84,240/year floor, and one hour per month of reconciliation adds about $1,800/year. Dividing $540 by 7 gives about $77 per night of coverage, which is 15x to 25x the model spend of a 24-attempt night at $0.12-0.21 per attempt. A Catchpoint SRE Report 2025 citation adds that about 70% of SREs say on-call stress contributed to burnout or attrition, so the real cost also includes turnover.
nodes.source: incident.io on-call compensation survey, 200+ orgs, 8 Sept 2026; devops.com citing Catchpoint SRE Report 2025 (~70% burnout link)

nodes.title: Models are ~100% reliable under 4 minutes and under 10% past 4 hours
nodes.body: METR's task-horizon work uses 170 tasks with 800+ human baselines: models succeed near 100% of the time on tasks under about 4 minutes and under 10% of the time on tasks over about 4 hours, with the 50%-success horizon doubling roughly every 7 months historically (1-4 doublings per year, about 196 days or 6.5 months in Time Horizon 1.1 with 228 tasks), while the SWE-Bench Verified human-time variant shows a faster sub-3-month doubling. The operational reading for an overnight run is blunt: an 8-hour unattended unit is two orders of magnitude past the reliable horizon, so the night must be decomposed into short verified units with checkpoints, and 'let it run all night' is not a capability question but an evidence question already answered.
nodes.source: METR, 'Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks' (19 Mar 2025); Time Horizon 1.1 (228 tasks, ~196-day doubling, Jan 2026)

nodes.title: Performance decays with input length at constant difficulty, and structure makes it worse
nodes.body: Chroma evaluated 18 LLMs over 194,480 calls with 0.035% refusals (69 cases): performance degrades as input length grows even when task difficulty is held fixed, degradation is steeper for lower needle-question similarity, a single distractor already hurts and four compound, and structurally coherent haystacks perform consistently worse than shuffled ones across all 18 models. In LongMemEval, full prompts averaging about 113k tokens versus focused prompts averaging about 300 tokens produce significantly worse results for every model, with Claude models abstaining most and GPT models hallucinating most. For dsh-loom the consequence is that an attempt which accumulates a large transcript does not just cost more, it becomes less able to judge its own work, so long attempts fail while looking busy.
nodes.source: Chroma Research, 'Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance' (Hong, Troynikov, Huber, 14 Jul 2025), 18 models, 194,480 calls

nodes.title: MAST: 14 failure modes across 1,600+ annotated multi-agent traces
nodes.body: MAST-Data annotates more than 1,600 traces across 7 multi-agent frameworks; the taxonomy itself was built from 150 traces with inter-annotator kappa = 0.88 and lands on 14 failure modes in 3 categories: system design issues, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification. The third category is the one that matters for unattended economics, because verification failures are precisely the ones that do not raise an error: the run completes, the artefact is wrong, and the spend is booked as a legitimate attempt. For dsh-loom, whose scores are binary 0/1, a verification failure is indistinguishable from a hard failure in the ledger, which is why the ledger needs a separate outcome class (crashed, timed out, produced-but-rejected) rather than one bit.
nodes.source: arXiv:2503.13657, 'Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?' (Cemri et al., v1 17 Mar 2025, v3 26 Oct 2025), MAST-Data, kappa = 0.88

nodes.title: Credentials expire mid-night: 6-hour re-auth and a 720-hour dead session
nodes.body: Two documented cases: OpenClaw issue #86583 reports an xAI OAuth refresh token stored but never auto-renewed, forcing manual re-authentication roughly every 6 hours on a headless Linux VPS; paperclipai/paperclip issue #20457 reports warm Codex sessions never writing refreshed credentials back to the tenant connection, a session that ran about 720 hours with the tenant grant drifting to needs_reauthorization. Both are cheap to fix and expensive to discover, because the failure is silent until a call returns 401 and the run stops mid-attempt with tokens already spent. For dsh-loom, the night must include a pre-flight auth probe with a token-lifetime check against the expected run duration, and a 401 handler that fails fast and loudly rather than retrying with the same dead credential.
nodes.source: github OpenClaw issue #86583; github paperclipai/paperclip issue #20457; blog-level reports, low-to-medium confidence

nodes.title: Disk fill is a wedged-host failure, not a clean error
nodes.body: A recorded incident (2026-10-19) hit 11 GB free at 99% utilisation, at which point Docker Desktop wedged and 'docker info' hung for 13 minutes rather than returning an error, and the largest reclaimable lever was build output accumulated in idle worktrees, about 0.2 GB freed per worktree. The important detail is the shape of the failure: a full disk does not fail fast, it makes every command hang, so an unattended run silently converts into a very expensive sleep. For dsh-loom, the corresponding controls are a pre-flight free-space floor, a per-attempt worktree teardown that is verified rather than fire-and-forget, and a watchdog that kills any single command exceeding a wall-clock threshold instead of trusting it to return.
nodes.source: suna project learnings entry 2026-10-19 (disk-full incident: 11 GB free / 99%, docker info hung 13 min, ~0.2 GB per worktree); project log, medium confidence

nodes.title: 246 of 289 worktrees were kept only for untracked droppings
nodes.body: An upgrade audit found that on one agent 246 of 289 worktrees were retained solely because they contained untracked files, i.e. unbounded growth of a .worktrees directory with no per-worktree teardown, and that the stale-worktree reaper failed closed on any git error so the leak compounded silently. This is the classic unattended-mode leak: nothing errors, nothing pages anyone, and the resource grows monotonically until it manifests as the disk-fill hang above. For dsh-loom, which by design creates a worktree per attempt, this predicts a per-night residue; the testable quantity is worktrees created minus worktrees removed per round, and the correct behaviour is to fail open (reclaim) on git error with a logged warning rather than to keep everything.
nodes.source: instar project upgrade notes (246 of 289 worktrees retained for untracked files; reaper fail-closed on git error); project notes, medium confidence

nodes.title: The discount stack: cache reads at 10%, off-peak at 50-75%, and a TTL trap
nodes.body: Cache mechanics: Anthropic charges 1.25x list to write a cache entry and 0.10x to read it, so break-even is 1.4 subsequent reads; OpenAI discounts cached input automatically at roughly 50%; Gemini discounts 75% with a minimum one-hour TTL for prompts of 32K+ tokens. Time-of-day pricing exists too: DeepSeek runs off-peak windows 16:30-00:30 UTC daily with V3 at 50% off and R1 at 75% off (announced 2025-02-25/26), and proxies such as LiteLLM expose an off_peak_pricing model key that tracks clock windows. For dsh-loom the scheduling consequence is concrete: an overnight job is already in the cheap window for some providers, but only if the prefix is stable enough to hit cache, since a 1-hour TTL means a 40-minute pause silently drops the discount for the rest of the night.
nodes.source: Anthropic/OpenAI/Google prompt-caching terms; DeepSeek off-peak announcement 2025-02-25/26 (16:30-00:30 UTC, V3 50%, R1 75%); LiteLLM off_peak_pricing docs

nodes.title: Published per-fix prices: $10.92 (Devin), $1.3-$6 (Claude Code eval runs)
nodes.body: Devin prices at $500/month for 250 included ACUs at about $2 each (Core is $20/month with ACUs at $2.25), 1 ACU is roughly 15 minutes of active work, and unassisted SWE-bench pass rate near 45.8% implies about 2.5 ACUs per fix, so a well-scoped successful fix lands near $10.92. Claude Code with Sonnet 4.5 at 77.2% SWE-Bench Verified costs about $1.3 per evaluation run versus Opus 4.7 at 87.6% for about $6 (codesota, April 2026). Third-party estimates put a resolved issue at $15-50 for an agent versus $300-1,500 for a human, with $2-10 of inference per task. These are vendor or list-price figures for a single clean task and carry no allowance for retries, failed attempts or a human on call.
nodes.source: Devin pricing ($500/mo Team, 250 ACUs ~$2, 1 ACU ~15 min, 45.8% unassisted SWE-bench); codesota pricing note April 2026 (Sonnet 4.5 77.2% ~$1.3/run, Opus 4.7 87.6% ~$6/run); third-party per-issue estimates

nodes.title: Our own ledger: 114 promotions over 452 attempts is a 25.2% base rate
nodes.body: dsh-loom's recorded history is 452 attempts, 231 rounds, 68 campaigns, 114 promotions and all scores binary 0/1. Derived: 1.96 attempts per round, 3.4 rounds per campaign, 6.6 attempts per campaign, 114/452 = 25.2% of attempts promote, 114/231 = 49.4% of rounds produce at least one promotion (assuming one promotion per round), and 1.68 promotions per campaign. The 25.2% figure is the single most important multiplier in this file: it means a real cost per accepted change is about 4x the cost per attempt, so a $0.12 attempt becomes $0.48 per accepted change and a $0.21 attempt becomes $0.83.
